module_title: Equations of Motion and Projectile Dynamics
introduction: When an object moves with a constant, uniform acceleration, its motion can be predicted mathematically using three standard equations. This level also introduces motion under gravity and the curved path of projectiles.

core_concepts.title: The Three Equations of Motion
core_concepts.description:
For a body starting with initial velocity (u), moving with constant acceleration (a), and reaching final velocity (v) in time (t) while covering displacement (s): 
1. First Equation: $v = u + at$ (Velocity-Time relation)
2. Second Equation: $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$ (Position-Time relation)
3. Third Equation: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ (Position-Velocity relation)

core_concepts.title: Free Fall (Motion under Gravity)
core_concepts.description: When an object falls freely towards the earth, its acceleration is 'g' (acceleration due to gravity, roughly $9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$). If a body is dropped from rest, $u = 0$. If a body is thrown upwards, gravity acts against it, so $a = -g$, and its final velocity at the highest point becomes zero ($v = 0$).

core_concepts.title: Projectile Motion
core_concepts.description: When an object is thrown into the air at an angle (other than 90 degrees), it moves under the influence of gravity alone along a curved path called a 'Parabola'. Examples: A javelin thrown by an athlete, a bullet fired from a gun.

core_concepts.title: Maximum Range and Height
core_concepts.description: To throw a projectile to the maximum horizontal distance (Maximum Range), it must be thrown at an angle of exactly 45 degrees. To throw it to the maximum vertical height, it must be thrown straight up at 90 degrees.

important_entities.name: Independence of Mass in Free Fall
important_entities.significance: If you drop a heavy iron ball and a light feather from the same height in a 'Vacuum' (where there is no air resistance), they will both hit the ground at the exact same time. Gravity accelerates all masses equally.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: Velocity at the Highest Point of a Projectile
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Exam Trap: 'What is the velocity of a projectile at its highest point?' Students often answer 'Zero'. FALSE. At the highest point, only the 'Vertical' velocity becomes zero. The 'Horizontal' velocity remains constant throughout the flight. So, total velocity is NOT zero.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Long jumpers aim for a 45-degree takeoff angle to cover the maximum horizontal distance.

exam_strategy_tips: In NDA and RRB exams, numericals often state 'a car starts from rest'. This is a code word meaning you must set initial velocity $u = 0$ in your equations.
